opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest obstacle isn't really model capability in the narrow sense. It's the feedback loop. For an agent to genuinely evolve itself, it needs a reliable signal telling it whether a change made it better or worse. In math or coding we have verifiers: the test passes or it doesn't, the proof checks or it doesn't. But most of the tasks we actually care about for agents are open-ended, long-horizon, and messy. The reward is delayed, it's noisy, and sometimes it's not even well-defined. Without a trustworthy evaluator, self-evolution easily turns into self-deception. The agent optimizes for whatever proxy it can see, and you get drift or reward hacking instead of real improvement.

The second issue is closely related, and it's memory and credit assignment over long trajectories. An agent might take hundreds of steps, call tools, and write and revise its own code or prompts. When something goes right or wrong at the end, figuring out which decision mattered is very hard. Humans learn from experience because we can reflect, abstract a lesson, and carry it forward. Current systems are still weak at turning raw experience into reusable, compressed knowledge that actually generalizes, rather than just piling up logs in a context window.

The third obstacle is stability. Once you let a system modify its own scaffolding, tools, or even weights, you open the door to compounding errors. A small bad update can cascade. So you need some notion of safe exploration: sandboxes, rollback, and conservative updates. That engineering is unglamorous, but I think it's essential.

So if I had to summarize: the bottleneck is less "can the model think" and more "can the system know when it has actually gotten better, and learn from that in a stable way." Whoever builds good environments and good verifiers for open-ended tasks will unlock a lot. In some sense, the environment and the evaluation become the new data. That's where I think a lot of the real research effort should go now.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest obstacle isn't the model itself. It's that we still haven't built a reliable loop where the agent can get a real signal from the environment and turn that signal into a durable improvement.

Let me break that into three pieces.

First, the feedback problem. In pretraining, the signal is cheap and dense: next token, billions of times. In RL for reasoning, we got lucky with math and code, because there's a verifier. You can check the answer. But for an agent operating in the open world, most of what matters doesn't have a clean verifier. Did this research plan make sense? Was this negotiation handled well? The agent can run for an hour and you still don't know if it did a good job. Without that signal, "self-evolving" is just a nice phrase. The agent can try things, but it can't tell which of its attempts were actually better, so it can't learn from them in a principled way.

Second, the credit assignment problem over long horizons. Even when you do get a signal at the end, a real task might involve hundreds of steps, tool calls, retries. Which step caused the failure? Today's methods are very bad at propagating reward back through that. So people end up giving dense human feedback, which is expensive and doesn't scale, or they give sparse outcome reward and the training is extremely inefficient. I think a lot of the near-term progress will come from learning better process models, essentially the agent building its own verifiers, rather than from bigger base models.

Third, and this is the one people underestimate: what does "evolve" even mean mechanically? Right now the options are updating weights, which is slow and expensive and risks degrading everything else, or writing things into memory and prompts, which is cheap but shallow. Neither is really like how a human engineer gets better over a year of work. We don't have a good intermediate layer where experience accumulates in a form the model can genuinely reuse. Until we figure that out, every "self-improving agent" demo is mostly a model plus a growing pile of notes.

And on top of all this there's a safety and evaluation question. If an agent is changing itself, you need to be able to measure whether it got better or worse, and in what directions. Our evaluations are already struggling to keep up with static models. With a moving target it's much harder.

So if I had to summarize it in one sentence: we know how to make the model stronger, but we don't yet know how to let the agent reliably make itself stronger, because the environment doesn't talk back clearly enough, and the agent doesn't have a good place to put what it learns.

astra-6.text:
I think the main obstacle is closing the feedback loop reliably. An agent can generate a new strategy or modify its own workflow, but how does it know that the change is actually an improvement? Completing one task successfully doesn’t necessarily mean it has learned something that will generalize.

For a self-evolving framework, you need trustworthy evaluation, a way to preserve useful experience, and a way to test changes without letting mistakes accumulate. Those pieces have to work together. Otherwise, you may get an agent that keeps changing, but isn’t consistently getting better.

So I would focus on the quality of the learning signal: can the agent identify what went wrong, make a targeted change, and demonstrate that the change helps on new tasks? That’s the loop we need to make dependable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main obstacle is closing the loop between experience, evaluation, and improvement. An agent can generate new strategies or revise its own workflow, but how does it know that a change actually makes it better? Success on one task might reflect luck, and optimizing for a narrow evaluator can produce behavior that fails elsewhere.

So the challenge is less about giving agents permission to modify themselves and more about building a reliable learning signal. They need to identify what went wrong, turn that experience into a useful change, and test whether the change generalizes without losing capabilities they already have. Until that loop is dependable, self-evolution will be difficult to distinguish from trial and error.
